windmill: Smock mill (Handorf)   
Title
Smock mill (Handorf)
Instance of windmill
Inception 1868
Located in the administrative territorial entity Handorf
This is a picture of the Baudenkmal (cultural heritage monument) according to the Cultural Heritage Protection Law of Lower Saxony with the ID 28828838 KDNI/28828838(andere) (Wikidata (P7900)).
This is a photograph of an architectural monument.
It is on the list of cultural monuments of Handorf.

Designation: Mill
Depicted part: House entrance
Construction time: 1868/69
Description: Smock mill with two-storey brick substructure built by miller and millwright Jürgen Meyer.

The octagonal mill hull is covered with thatch.
The windmill is part of the Lower Saxon Mill Road.
  • In 1907 Georg Meyer installed a suction gas engine.
  • In 1921 the mill was completely renewed by Wilhelm Meyer. The technical equipment was equipped with a roller mill, a gristmill and a milling gear.
  • In the 1960s, Gerhard Meyer shut down the business and sold the mill.
  • In 1983, after several changes of ownership, Prof. Dr. Volker Schütz bought the mill and converted it into a residential mill.
  • In 1998 during the spring storms the wooden sails, which had been renewed in 1989, partially broke off due to wood rot and were replaced by steel rods in 2000.

Place:  Municipality Handorf ▷ Collective municipality Bardowick ▷ Rural district Lüneburg ▷ Lower Saxony ▷ Germany ▷ Europe
Location: Hauptstraße

House number: 57

ImageDescription.value:
Cat in Arkadi Monastery (Μονή Αρκαδίου), Amnatos, Crete, Greece
The Arkadi Monastery on Crete, completed in its current Renaissance splendor in the 16th century, is the central symbol of the Cretan struggle for freedom. Its history is inextricably linked to November 9, 1866: during the Cretan uprising against Ottoman rule, nearly 1,000 people, mostly women and children, sought refuge behind the monastery walls.
After a two-day siege by superior forces, Ottoman troops stormed the complex. To avoid captivity and shame, the defenders blew up the powder magazine themselves on the abbot’s orders. This self-sacrifice sparked horror and solidarity around the world and ultimately led to the independence of Crete. Today, Arkadi Monastery is a national shrine, whose ruins of the powder magazine and bullet-riddled iconostasis serve as memorials to the resistance.
